title: ActiveKV
subtitle: An inference-memory layer for vLLM: the conversation's history in host RAM, the GPU as a bounded working set

stats.label: exact cells bit-identical to fully resident attention at the port, 12 of 12 hybrid
former Python dispatch sites still in Python, kept by a cited framework contract
lower time to first token than stock vLLM, single request, every context length
faster cold 32K-token prefill from the Xe2 kernel patches

lede: Every serving engine I have worked with assumes a model's working memory lives on the GPU. That assumption is why a 32 GB card decides how much context a model can hold. I decided to remove it. ActiveKV is an inference-memory layer I architected for vLLM: the conversation's attention history lives in pinned host RAM, and the GPU keeps a bounded, budgeted working set. On one Intel Arc Pro GPU, a 27-billion-parameter model serves 128,000-token histories. On a single 8,000-token request it beats stock vLLM on time to first token, inter-token latency and throughput.
quote: Context length should be a host-memory budget, and it should stop being a hardware limit.
evidence: KV-cache offload for LLM inference: attention history in host RAM with the GPU as a bounded working set, on one Intel Arc Pro GPU with 32 GB.
C++ and native ports with parity proof: a Python runtime ported to C++ with 13 of 13 exact cells bit-identical and 1 of 867 dispatch sites left in Python under a cited contract.
Inference serving architecture: 12-22% lower time to first token than stock vLLM on a single request at every context length.
Intel GPU and SYCL/oneAPI engineering: kernel patches on Xe2 for 20% faster cold 32K-token prefill, each gated on identical outputs.
vLLM internals: delivered as compiled binaries plus a patch to the user's own vLLM, with no Python of mine in the release payload.
Observability and instrumentation: per-token tracing from scheduler to device to client at selectable levels, with its own overhead measured.
author: Corey James
